items.label: Data acquisition or calibration infrastructure (firmware, time sync, or calibration constants) underwent a silent drift or unlogged update between days 10–11, introducing a ramping correction parameter that affects all four streams with apparatus-specific gain factors. The negative autocorrelations reflect residual quantization or rounding artifacts in the DAQ system after the update.

Resonator_obs has higher sensitivity to a slow environmental ramp (temperature, facility thermal mass, or barometric pressure transient) that began before day 1 or ramped throughout days 1–22; other apparatus are less sensitive or noisier.

Statistical artifact: post-baseline sample size (n=18–34) is too small and the observed z-scores are consistent with chance fluctuation in a short window, especially given multiple hypothesis tests on the baseline data already performed.
Residual: unrecognized systematic effect specific to Meridian's environment, measurement protocol, or apparatus interaction not yet distinguished from noise.

Genuine environmental drift affecting all apparatus with apparatus-specific gain: a slow physical change at Meridian (temperature, magnetic field, gravitational gradient, or instrumental warm-up over 13 days) is shifting all four measurement streams downward, but by different amounts because each apparatus has different sensitivity or thermal mass.
Insufficient baseline period and statistical flukes: 10 days is too short to distinguish structured variation from noise aliasing and chance correlation peaks

Negative self-autocorrelations (pendulum_lab −0.407, pendulum_obs −0.296) and weak cross-stream correlations indicate high-frequency measurement noise dominates the signal; all four streams show genuine statistical noise fluctuation, not a true environmental phenomenon. Resonator_obs z = −1.96 is a rare event (2.3% tail) driven by larger sample size (n=174) allowing noise variance to accumulate into statistical significance. The uniform direction (all negative) across streams is coincidental (6% chance if independent).

Residual: An unconsidered interaction or Meridian-specific phenomenon not captured by the above. Candidates include unrecognized coupling between the four apparatus (e.g., shared air circulation, acoustic coupling, or magnetic cross-talk); a Meridian-specific gravitational or tidal transient; or a measurement artifact from data post-processing (e.g., smoothing filter, outlier rejection, or unit conversion) applied after day 10 that I have not yet identified.
Unrecognized instrumental artifact: digital quantization, rounding, or firmware timing in data logging creates pseudo-patterns

Resonator_obs has higher sensitivity to a slow environmental ramp (temperature, facility thermal mass, or barometric pressure transient) that began before day 1 or ramped throughout days 1–22; other apparatus are less sensitive or noisier.

Instrumental settling or calibration drift was underway during the baseline period itself (days 1–10); baseline is contaminated and should not be treated as the true zero-point. All four apparatus continued a pre-existing ramp through day 19+, visible now as a consistent post-baseline shift only because n is larger post-baseline.

A procedural or environmental change near day 10–11 (observer schedule shift, HVAC restart, facility maintenance, or external noise source activation) introduced a measurement bias affecting resonator_obs more strongly than other apparatus; bias magnitude correlates with apparatus sensitivity to vibration or electromagnetic interference.

Shared data acquisition infrastructure (firmware, network time synchronization, calibration routine) underwent silent drift or minor update between days 10–11, introducing a systematic bias in all four streams with apparatus-specific gain factors; resonator_obs gain is highest.

Resonator_obs is the only stream with sufficient post-baseline sample size (n=174) to resolve a genuine noise-dominated fluctuation; the downward drift in all four streams is a statistical artifact driven by random variance, not a true phenomenon.

Residual: An unconsidered phenomenon or interaction specific to Meridian environment or the apparatus configuration. Candidates include: (1) facility thermal mass transient with a time constant that defeats simple autocorrelation but couples all four instruments; (2) a phase-shifted or filtered environmental signal (e.g., barometric pressure or seismic noise) that appears as negative autocorrelation after high-pass filtering; (3) a systematic interaction or feedback between the four apparatus that I have not yet recognized; (4) a Meridian-specific gravitational, tidal, or magnetic anomaly with apparatus-specific coupling.

Contaminated baseline: instrumental settling ramp present throughout days 1–19, not arrested at day 10. Baseline (days 1–10) captures the warm-up phase of all four instruments; apparent drift post-baseline is an artifact of comparing mid-ramp to later-ramp. Resonator_obs significance emerges only because it accumulated n=174 post-baseline trials, enough to resolve a 0.014 cycle/beat shift that smaller n streams cannot detect despite having the same underlying ramp.

Common environmental ramp (temperature, facility thermal mass, or slow barometric pressure change) began before day 1 or ramped uniformly throughout days 1–22+. All four apparatus are sensitive to this ramp, but resonator_obs is 2–3× more sensitive (higher gain to the environmental coupling). Post-baseline means lie on the continuation of the baseline trend with apparatus-specific gains. Negative autocorrelations result from high measurement noise overlaying a low-SNR environmental signal; noise dominates autocorrelation structure.

Procedural or environmental change near day 10–11 (HVAC restart, observer schedule shift, facility access pattern, or external noise source activation) introduced a measurement bias affecting all four streams. Resonator_obs exhibits the largest bias because it couples more strongly to vibration or electromagnetic interference. The ramp appearance post-baseline results from thermal re-equilibration *after* the bias introduction, creating a smooth-looking drift that masks an underlying step.

Data acquisition or calibration infrastructure (shared firmware, network time sync, or calibration database) underwent silent drift or unlogged update between days 10–11, introducing systematic bias in all four streams with apparatus-specific gain factors; resonator_obs gain highest. The bias is not a discrete step but a ramping correction parameter (e.g., a temperature-dependent gain multiplier in firmware that drifted over hours).

Negative self-autocorrelations (pendulum_lab −0.407, pendulum_obs −0.296) and weak cross-stream correlations indicate high-frequency measurement noise dominates the signal; all four streams show genuine statistical noise fluctuation, not a true environmental phenomenon. Resonator_obs z = −1.96 is a rare event (2.3% tail) driven by larger sample size (n=174) allowing noise variance to accumulate into statistical significance. The uniform direction (all negative) across streams is coincidental (6% chance if independent).

Residual: An unconsidered interaction or Meridian-specific phenomenon. Candidates include: (1) facility thermal mass transient with multi-scale time constant that defeats simple autocorrelation analysis; (2) phase-shifted or high-pass filtered environmental signal (e.g., seismic noise or barometric resonance) that appears as negative autocorrelation after filtering; (3) systematic measurement protocol element (e.g., cyclic observer bias, diurnal facility activity pattern, or apparatus warm-up routine) that creates negative autocorrelation; (4) unrecognized feedback or coupling between the four apparatus; (5) Meridian-specific gravitational, tidal, or magnetic anomaly with apparatus-specific coupling. The negative self-autocorrelations are a critical clue: they are inconsistent with both pure noise and smooth environmental ramps, and their origin is not explained by current hypotheses.

Measurement protocol contains an unrecognized oscillating or cyclic observer bias element (e.g., fatigue cycle, instrument warm-up routine, or systematic correction procedure) that introduces negative autocorrelation on a 6–10 day timescale while a separate slow environmental or instrumental drift produces the uniform post-baseline shift.

Instrumental warm-up or thermal settling ramp was present throughout days 1–22+, not arrested at day 10. Baseline (days 1–10) and post-baseline both lie on a continuous downward ramp with apparatus-specific slopes. Negative autocorrelations arise from high-frequency measurement noise overlaid on a low-SNR ramp; noise dominates lag-structure, producing anti-correlation when noise amplitude is large relative to signal drift rate.

External environmental signal (temperature, facility vibration, barometric pressure, or seismic noise) underwent a phase shift or resonant coupling near day 10–11, introducing a high-pass filtered or oscillating component that is invisible to direct inspection but visible in negative autocorrelation structure. The signal couples with apparatus-specific gains, producing the uniform drift direction and resonator_obs asymmetry. True environmental ramp continues underneath.

Data acquisition or calibration infrastructure (firmware, time sync, or calibration constants) underwent a silent drift or unlogged update between days 10–11, introducing a ramping correction parameter that affects all four streams with apparatus-specific gain factors. The negative autocorrelations reflect residual quantization or rounding artifacts in the DAQ system after the update.

All observed patterns (uniform drift, negative autocorrelations, weak cross-correlations, resonator_obs asymmetry) are artifacts of natural measurement noise and statistical fluctuation; no single environmental or procedural cause underlies all four streams. The uniform negative drift is coincidental (≈6% chance); resonator_obs z = −1.85 reflects sample size (n=174), not a true phenomenon.

Residual: An unconsidered interaction or Meridian-specific phenomenon not captured by the above. Candidates include unrecognized coupling between the four apparatus (e.g., shared air circulation, acoustic coupling, or magnetic cross-talk); a Meridian-specific gravitational or tidal transient; or a measurement artifact from data post-processing (e.g., smoothing filter, outlier rejection, or unit conversion) applied after day 10 that I have not yet identified.
